text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
--- Employment officials report an increasing lack of skilled workers in the construction industry and economists now fear that the industry may face increasing pressure for higher wages in future.

--- TV company Broadcast Danmark, 100 percent owned by Scandinavian Broadcast whose largest shareholder is ABC/Disney, hopes to produce and buy TV programmes worth 200 million crowns over the next 'couple of years'. Broadcast Danmark is mainly known for its Copenhagen TV station Kanal 2 which started uncoded broadcasting two weeks ago almost doubling its number of viewers.

--- Local authorities are to increase taxes by a total of 3.2 billion crowns. The money will be spent on care for children and the elderly, purchase of more computers for primary schools, hospitals and psychiatry.

--- Copenhagen's Tivoli entertainment park is to work with US Disney group development company Imagineering, meaning among other things that Disney is to train Tivoli staff at its Disney University in California and at the Tivoli site. At the same time Disneyland in, California, is to turn some of its own space into Tivoli-like areas. Tivoli CEO Lars Liebst says he will maintain the present Tivoli concept and atmosphere, but still develop the park so that it does not turn into a museum.
--- Denmark is to grant 1.2 million crowns for human rights and the media in Bosnia. The money will be given to independent media and human rights organisations all over the region.

--- Denmark's largest shipyard, Odense Staalskibsvaerft, owned by shipping group A.P. Moeller is turning to the EU to stop further German state subsidies to its shipyards. Denmark says it is one of the few countries in the European Union to respect present rules on shipyard subsidies and the industry now feels threatened by subsidised shipyards abroad which are able to sell cheaper than Danish yards.
--- The Danish Supervisory Authority of Financial Affairs expects more high street banks to fail or seek niche positions by the end of the decade, due to increased competition.
